content.title: About
content.content: Raw asparagus consists of the young shoots of Asparagus officinalis, cultivated in temperate climates. It has a delicate, slightly nutty flavor and a crisp texture. Asparagus can be eaten raw in salads or briefly cooked for a tender bite.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Asparagus is one of the oldest cultivated vegetables, with a history of over 2,000 years.
In ancient Roman medicine it was used as a diuretic and liver tonic.
Fresh asparagus season runs from early spring to early summer.
There are several varieties: green, white (grown in darkness), and purple.
Raw asparagus is a rich source of folate, important for cell division.

items.title: Rich in folate
items.content: Folate supports DNA synthesis and is especially important for pregnant women.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Raw asparagus provides very few calories, making it ideal for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: It supplies vitamin C, vitamin E and glutathione, which protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Potassium and dietary fiber help maintain normal blood pressure and cholesterol levels.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: While not a major protein source, asparagus contributes to daily protein intake.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to asparagus.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: Large amounts of raw asparagus can cause gas and discomfort due to its fiber content.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Asparagus contains oxalates, which in excess may contribute to kidney stone formation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice raw asparagus thinly and add to salads, smoothies, or marinate it. It can also be briefly blanched in boiling water for a softer texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store asparagus in the refrigerator wrapped in a slightly damp towel and placed in a plastic bag. Use within 3–5 days. Discard if yellow spots or off‑odors develop.
